glosses: To leave or escape.

examples.text: In case of fire, get out by the nearest exit.
You have to get out on a bull to succeed in a rodeo.

The end comes, and then drums, drums in the deep. I wonder what that means. The last thing written is in a trailing scrawl of elf-letters: they are coming. glosses: To come out of a situation; to escape a fate.

examples.text: Never take life seriously. Nobody gets out alive anyway.

glosses: To be released, especially from hospital or prison.

examples.text: He's been in prison for six months, but he gets out next week.

glosses: To remove one's money from an investment; to end an investment.

examples.text: I think copper prices will plummet this fall, so I'm getting out while I can.

glosses: To help (someone) leave.

examples.text: We must get the children out first.

glosses: To take (something) from its container or storage place, so as to use or display it.

examples.text: Get the playing cards out and we'll have a game of snap.
It's time to get the Christmas decorations out.

glosses: To leave the inside of a vehicle such as a car. (Note: for public transport, get off is more common.)

examples.text: I'll get out at the end of the road and walk from there.

glosses: To become known.

examples.text: Somehow the secret got out.
We have to act before that fact gets out on us.

glosses: To spend free time out of the house.

examples.text: You work too hard. You should get out more.

glosses: To publish or make available; to disseminate.

examples.text: The organization has just gotten their newsletter out.
This candidate is struggling to get her message out.

glosses: To say with difficulty.

examples.text: He could hardly get the words out for the tears.

glosses: To remove or eliminate (dirt or stains).

examples.text: This detergent will get most household stains out.

glosses: To end.

examples.text: School gets out in the afternoon.

glosses: Commanding a person to leave.

examples.text: Get out! I never want to see you in here again!

glosses: Indicating incredulity.

examples.text: "Giants in armour, sir. Hundred feet high. Three legs and a body like 'luminium, with a mighty great head in a hood, sir." "Get out!" said the lieutenant. "What confounded nonsense!".

glosses: Expressing disapproval or disgust, especially after a bad joke.

examples.text: Just get out.

glosses: To overcome.

examples.text: I'm trying to get over my fear of flying.

glosses: To recover (from).

examples.text: I'm having problems getting over a bad cold.

glosses: To forget and move on; to calm down regarding something.

examples.text: She was in love with me for 10 years, and still hasn't got over the fact that the feeling wasn't mutual.

glosses: To manipulate (someone); to get around (someone); to improve one's own standing at another's expense.

examples.text: We need a plan to get over Mr. Smith.

glosses: To successfully communicate; to get across.

examples.text: In our lectures we need to get over the importance of online safety.

glosses: To score a try.

examples.text: Ireland got their second try not long before half-time with O'Leary, an injury doubt all week with a stiff back, just about getting over for a try which was confirmed by the video referee.

glosses: To impress someone; to achieve a goal; to be successful.

examples.text: The concert went well, and we really got over with the talent scout.

glosses: To establish a connection with the audience as a character or faction.
To use a drug one is addicted to; to provide an addict with a dose.

examples.text: She needs to get over every day.
He can get me over.

glosses: To have sex.

examples.text: But sith this wretched woman ouercome / Of anguish, rather then of crime hath beene,
